claims.statement: The annotation value tree mirrors the schema: AnnotationValueTree is a map keyed by node name holding InstanceNode[] (bounded by min/max); each InstanceNode may carry a value (if a field) and/or children. emptyValue defaults false for boolean and null otherwise; makeInstance/initTree build fresh instances recursively at min.

The on-disk project format is split: project.json holds only meta (schema/protocol/paper metadata, no annotations/reviews/aiUsage/equal/consolidationSync), while annotations/<paperId>/ holds consolidated.json, reviewer-<n>.json, marks-consolidated.json, and marks-<n>.json. Screening projects use screening-<n>.json / screening-consolidated.json prefixes instead of reviewer-/consolidated.

splitProjectFiles is a pure side-effect-free function returning {meta, files} where each ProjectFileEntry has relPath and a text of null meaning the file should not exist (caller deletes it if present on disk). The Electron adapter's saveProject and the git layer's toSplitProject perform the actual fs writes/deletes.

aiUsage, equal, and consolidationSync are not split per reviewer even in a multi-reviewer project; aiUsage is one array for the whole paper, equal is a consolidation-time concept, and consolidationSync describes Consolidation's own automatic steps, so all three ride in the consolidated.json file regardless of which tree they describe.

The in-memory Project type carries version, title, provenance, protocol, schemaInfo, schema (ResolvedDef[]), aiEnabled, finishCheckbox, reviewers, papers, screening, and extra. provenance/protocol/schemaInfo are required-not-optional (T | null) so constructing a Project without deciding what to do with them is a type error, not a silent drop, which matters at mergeProjects.

protocol and schemaInfo live at the project root, not under config, because config is a strict zod object rebuilt from scratch on every save and would silently drop anything hand-added under it. They are loosely typed in zod and parsed structurally by parseProtocol/parseSchemaInfo.

For a screening project the schema is derived from config.screening.reasons (screeningSchemaDefs) on every load and config.schema is ignored; the derived schema is written back on save so the file stays self-describing but the two can never drift. Project.screening is the single source of truth.

Paper repeats the single-tree-vs-per-reviewer split four times (annotations/reviews, marks/reviewMarks, finished/reviewsFinished) because each reviewer owns their own reading independently and the consolidated seat owns the reconciled record that ships. In a single-reviewer project the per-reviewer maps stay empty.

Paper.finished is stored, not derived from the data: a full tree is a fact about the form, not a judgement that the extraction is right. It is not re-derived on load, so a later edit that empties a field leaves the flag standing while the dot stops being green (the paper list requires both) — nothing silently un-declares a reviewer's declaration.

StoredAlignment records which of each reviewer's repeated entries are the same entry as an explicit mapping rather than by reordering reviewers' arrays (the pre-v1.7 approach that wrote Consolidation bookkeeping into other people's data). alignedReviews projects reviewers' trees through the mapping as a throwaway lined-up view without touching stored trees. It is persisted because slot N must keep meaning the same thing once a consolidator commits an answer under it.

loadProject is the single load entry point: it depth-guards first (MAX_JSON_DEPTH 200, before any recursive walker), parses with zod (ZodError/RangeError become friendly ProjectLoadError), resolves the schema, checks duplicate paper ids, and builds each Paper with defensive parse helpers that drop malformed entries rather than throwing.

normalizeTree reconciles a value tree against the schema: coerces each present instance's structure to the def, pads up to min (at least 1), and clamps to max. It adopts shorthand shapes (bare primitive, single entry where a list is wanted) as the value rather than dropping them, because this walk rewrites the file and discarding would let the next save overwrite a real answer with null. Keys the schema no longer knows about are not dropped: orphanedNodes carries them through verbatim (when they hold a real answer), so renaming a field in project.json does not destroy the answers other reviewers recorded under the old name.

normalizeReviews backfills a skeleton tree for every reviewer 1..reviewerCount who has no tree, so a reviewer's first annotation is a value-on-existing-line change in a git diff rather than a new field appearing. It never removes a key for a reviewer number above reviewerCount: lowering the count hides that reviewer's tree but must not delete it.

Edits (setFieldValue/addInstance/removeInstance) route through currentTree to the correct seat's tree: single-reviewer or Consolidation seat writes paper.annotations; a numbered reviewer writes paper.reviews[currentReviewer] (lazily created on first write). setFieldValue coalesces consecutive edits of the same field into one undo step.

removeInstance shifts canonical paths of survivors after splicing a non-last entry, because every structure addresses a field instance by canonical path with an embedded index. It rewrites linked-field mark paths, AI marks, paper.equal entries, and deferred consolidations via shiftCanonicalPath (dropping those that named the removed instance).

pruneTree drops only trailing empty instances from each list (required instances up to min are always kept). Non-trailing empties are kept because position carries meaning: Consolidation lines reviewers' lists up by index, and closing a gap would silently re-point the alignment at the wrong entries on the next load. A trailing instance is also kept when it holds orphaned answers under child names the schema no longer knows about (holdsOrphans), so dropping trailing empties does not delete the answers a node losing its children was meant to preserve.

serializedTree(schema, tree) is hasContent(schema, tree) ? pruneTree(schema, tree) : {} — an empty normalized tree exists in memory to bind the form to the schema but does not belong in a file until a reviewer has recorded an answer or a schema edit has orphaned one. hasContent is hasAnnotations || treeHoldsOrphans, so removing the one field a reviewer filled in is not what deletes their work. This rule is shared by serializeProject and splitProjectFiles.

serializeProject and splitProjectFiles sort papers by plain case-sensitive string comparison on id (comparePapers), which is deterministic and locale-independent, unlike title ordering which also drifts if a reviewer edits a title after first sort.

deepEqualJson is structural JSON equality: order-independent for object keys, order-sensitive for arrays, exactly JSON's notion otherwise. It is deliberately not a text comparison so that whitespace, indentation, and key-order rewrites (which serializeProject freely rewrites on every save) never look like a semantic change. It is shared across the codebase: git/merge.ts uses it for three-way field-change decisions and git/changes.ts uses it for bookkeeping-field and schema/provenance/protocol diff checks, so a second implementation of the same notion would be a bug waiting to happen.

isLegacyProjectShape detects whether a parsed project.json uses the old single-file shape (any paper carries annotations or reviews inline). assembleLegacyProjectJson reassembles a meta-only body plus per-paper files back into the legacy whole-project shape loadProject already parses, so the read path reuses loadProject unchanged.

Per-paper-per-reviewer files are written only when the tree holds content (hasContent — a real answer or orphaned answers under a removed schema node) or the reviewer's finished flag is set, and deleted (text: null) when empty. marks files are written when the mark list is non-empty. A null text is the delete signal: splitProjectFiles is pure, so the caller deletes any on-disk file whose entry is null.

splitProjectFiles emits reviewer slots as the union of 1..reviewers and every reviewer number parseReviews/parseReviewsFinished kept (including ones above the current count), so lowering config.reviewers does not delete that reviewer's tree and it reappears if the count is raised back — the same contract normalizeReviews makes for the in-memory shape.

annotationState defines a single five-state vocabulary (untouched/partial/complete/finished/flagged) behind the paper list dot, its state filter, and its finished counter, so they can never disagree. The two inputs are independent: completeness (a fact about the data) and finished (a reviewer's declaration); annotationState is the one place they combine.

The flagged state (declared finished while a required field is empty) is re-evaluated from current data on every read, so it flips to and from finished on its own as fields empty and refill — nothing has to be saved and no separate invalidation step exists. It is only reachable in a schema that marks something required (hasRequiredFields).

completenessApplies is the one gate behind the dot's color, the finished checkbox, and the filter dropdown. Only a screening project is excluded (it has its own tri-state marker and a derived schema marking nothing required). Consolidation is included, which is why the gate needs no seat argument: the consolidated tree's tick routes to Paper.finished like a lone reviewer's.

finishCheckboxLabel(isConsolidation) returns 'Consolidation finished' for the Consolidation seat and 'Annotation finished' otherwise — one definition because the paper list's complete tooltip sends the reader to that control by name.

When config.finishCheckbox is false, nobody signs off, so a fulfilled schema is finished and the stored tick is not read at all (it may hold a stale declaration). complete and flagged are both unreachable; any ticks recorded while it was on are kept in the file so turning it back on restores them.

AnnotationFilter is all/open/in-progress/finished/issues — four buckets over the five states. open is every paper whose box is not ticked; in-progress is its started subset (decided from touched, not state, since a Yes/No-only paper is touched while its dot stays untouched); issues is flagged. annotationFiltersFor drops issues when no paper can reach it (finishCheckbox false); matchesFilter is the single mapping and a null (screening) state matches only all.

loadProject uses a uniform defensive-parse convention for hand-editable fields (reviews, aiUsage, equal, alignment, consolidationSync, marks, provenance, protocol, schemaInfo): malformed entries are dropped, never thrown over. The one exception is parseScreening, whose reasons are the schema's enum and cannot be degraded past — an empty result is a load error, not an empty list.

loadProject depth-guards the parsed JSON (exceedsDepth, MAX_JSON_DEPTH 200) before any recursive walker runs, because zod validation, resolveDefs, normalizeTree, deepEqualJson, and serializeProject are all recursive and blow the stack between a few hundred and a few thousand levels; without the guard a deeply nested hand-edited file escapes the function's throws-ProjectLoadError contract as a raw RangeError.

For a screening project splitProjectFiles names per-reviewer files screening-<n>.json and the consolidated file screening-consolidated.json instead of reviewer-/consolidated — same layout, a different prefix so screening decisions and full annotations are distinguishable in the folder. marks-* files keep the same name in both modes.

ProjectProvenance records where a project's papers came from when built by importing from another project (kind:'screening-import', source file name never an absolute path, importedAt, and a counts snapshot of included/undecided/excluded/carried at import time) so a shared git-committed file can answer 'where did this come from' without the source file reachable.

Paper.consolidationSync is an optional digest pair (djb2 hash of each reviewer's pruned tree, joined with a digest of the pruned consolidated tree) recorded by consolidationMark(schema, paper) after Consolidation's automatic matching/adoption steps run on a paper; it is compared on re-entering the seat so unchanged reviewer answers never re-trigger those steps and overwrite a consolidator's deliberate edit.

Migration from the legacy single-file shape to the split layout is silent and automatic on the next explicit save: project:save and the git layer's toSplitProject always write through splitProjectFiles, which produces the split layout regardless of the shape the file was read in. Opening a project never writes to disk by itself — the old shape-migration that re-serialized and resaved on open was removed, because a schema field added after the file was written made every paper's file look changed and produced a whole-folder diff in a shared repository from a reviewer who only looked.
